summary: The note describes phosphenes, the perception of light without light entering the eye, covering their etymology and the many ways they can be induced. It surveys causes including mechanical pressure on the eyes, everyday events like sneezing, electrical and magnetic stimulation of the visual system, medications, and radiation. It also covers the prevailing mechanism theory, an anthropological claim about Upper Paleolithic art, and research on visual prostheses and the BrainNet brain-to-brain communication experiment.
one_line: Overview of phosphenes, the sensation of seeing light without light entering the eye, and their causes, mechanisms and research uses.
key_facts: A phosphene is the phenomenon of seeing light without light entering the eye, from the Greek words phos (light) and phainein (to show).
Pressure phosphenes, caused by rubbing or applying pressure on or near the closed eyes, have been known since antiquity and described by the Greeks.
Isaac Newton detailed an example in which gently pressing the side of one's eye produces a colored ring of light on the opposite side.
The name 'phosphene' was coined by J. B. H. Savigny, better known as the ship's surgeon of the wrecked French frigate Méduse.
Serre d'Uzes first employed phosphenes to test retinal function prior to cataract surgery.
Neurologist Otfrid Foerster reported phosphenes created by electrical stimulation of the brain as early as 1929.
Brindley and Lewin (1968) inserted a matrix of stimulating electrodes directly into the visual cortex of a 52-year-old blind female to create phosphenes.
Brindley and Rushton (1974) used phosphenes to depict Braille spots as a visual prosthesis.
Phosphenes produced by intense, changing magnetic fields such as transcranial magnetic stimulation are known as magnetophosphenes.
Patients undergoing radiotherapy have reported seeing blue flashes of light, a phenomenon shown to resemble Cherenkov radiation.
Phosphenes can be caused by some medications, such as Ivabradine.
Most vision researchers believe phosphenes result from normal activity of the visual system after stimulation of one of its parts by a stimulus other than light.

In 1988, David Lewis-Williams and T. A. Dowson argued that non-figurative Upper Paleolithic art depicts visions of phosphenes and neurological 'form constants', probably enhanced by hallucinogenic drugs.
The BrainNet system produces phosphenes using transcranial magnetic stimulation, with signals detected by electroencephalography (EEG) and delivered by TMS.
In the BrainNet experiment, five groups of three people were used and the experiment achieved 81% success.
